desc:
A root-to-leaf path starts at the root and follows child links down to a leaf, a node that has no children. Given a binary tree and an integer target, decide whether some root-to-leaf path has node values that add up to exactly target. Return true or false.

The path must end at a leaf: a node that merely has a missing child on one side is not a leaf. The empty tree has no paths, so the answer is false for it.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). Node values can be negative in this problem, so a missing child is written as 1000 (real node values always lie between -500 and 500, so the marker can never be confused with a value). The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing 1000 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with 1000. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, 1000, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [5, 4, 8, 11, 1000, 13, 4, 7, 2, 1000, 1000, 1000, 1] and target = 22 the answer is true (the path 5 → 4 → 11 → 2). For tree = [1, 2] and target = 1 the answer is false: the only leaf is 2, and the path to it sums to 3.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, missing child written as 1000, no trailing 1000)
hints: Every root-to-leaf path is determined by its last node. Can you know the sum of the path ending at a node when you reach it?
The sum of the path to a child is the sum of the path to its parent plus the child's value. Carry that running sum downward.
Walk the tree top to bottom. At a node with no children, compare its running sum with target. Remember that a node with exactly one child is not a leaf, and that the empty tree gives false.
editorial: Define the running sum of a node as the sum of all values on the path from the root to that node. The root's running sum is its own value, and a child's running sum is its parent's running sum plus its own value. A root-to-leaf path with sum target exists exactly when some leaf has running sum target.

In the level-order array a parent always comes before its children, so one forward pass over the real nodes computes every running sum with no recursion. Check the sums of the nodes without children. A recursive version that subtracts the node value from target on the way down and tests for 0 at a leaf is equivalent. The two traps are treating a node with a single child as a leaf and forgetting that values can be negative, so you cannot stop early when the running sum passes the target.
Each node is visited once: O(n) time, and the array of running sums takes O(n) space.
